verses.text: Then Job answered,
“Listen diligently to my speech. Let this be your consolation.
Allow me, and I also will speak; After I have spoken, mock on.
As for me, is my complaint to man? Why shouldn’t I be impatient?
Look at me, and be astonished. Lay your hand on your mouth.
When I remember, I am troubled. Horror takes hold of my flesh.
“Why do the wicked live, become old, yes, and grow mighty in power?
Their child is established with them in their sight, their offspring before their eyes.
Their houses are safe from fear, neither is the rod of God upon them.
Their bulls breed without fail. Their cows calve, and don’t miscarry.
They send out their little ones like a flock. Their children dance.
They sing to the tambourine and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the pipe.
They spend their days in prosperity. In an instant they go down to Sheol.
They tell God, ‘Depart from us, for we don’t want to know about your ways.
What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? What profit should we have, if we pray to him?’
Behold, their prosperity is not in their hand. The counsel of the wicked is far from me.
“How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out, that their calamity comes on them, that God distributes sorrows in his anger?
How often is it that they are as stubble before the wind, as chaff that the storm carries away?
You say, ‘God lays up his iniquity for his children.’ Let him recompense it to himself, that he may know it.
Let his own eyes see his destruction. Let him drink of the wrath of the Almighty.
For what does he care for his house after him, when the number of his months is cut off?
“Shall any teach God knowledge, since he judges those who are high?
One dies in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet.
His pails are full of milk. The marrow of his bones is moistened.
Another dies in bitterness of soul, and never tastes of good.
They lie down alike in the dust. The worm covers them.
“Behold, I know your thoughts, the devices with which you would wrong me.
For you say, ‘Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in which the wicked lived?’
Haven’t you asked wayfaring men? Don’t you know their evidences,
that the evil man is reserved to the day of calamity, That they are led out to the day of wrath?
Who shall declare his way to his face? Who shall repay him what he has done?
Yet he will be borne to the grave. Men shall keep watch over the tomb.
The clods of the valley shall be sweet to him. All men shall draw after him, as there were innumerable before him.
So how can you comfort me with nonsense, because in your answers there remains only falsehood?”

footnotes.content: Job takes his turn again. Notice the patience of this conversation—even in exasperation, one man still opens his mouth to another. The Lord will do the same with Job, waiting to be heard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let this be your consolation"—how gentle an irony. Job knows his friends have tried to comfort him with doctrine when what he needs is honesty. Sometimes the deepest gift is permission to speak what's really true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job grants his friends permission to mock him after he's done—a kind of humility wrapped in defiance. He will speak his piece, then let them laugh if they must. There's courage in that.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Is my complaint to man?" Job turns his gaze upward. His real quarrel is not with Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar—it is with the God who seems silent. That directness, painful as it is, is closer to prayer than polite theology.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Look at me, and be astonished. Lay your hand on your mouth." Job asks for what he truly needs: recognition of his suffering, and silence. Not answers. Not explanations. Just presence and the grace to be still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Job remembers his former life and sees it now against his skin's corruption, the horror overtakes him physically. His whole body carries the knowledge. Christ too would sweat blood as He remembered what was coming—suffering isn't meant to be merely intellectual.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The central question Job cannot avoid: "Why do the wicked live?" It's the one thing none of his friends have answered, and it burns. There is no shallow answer to this. Even the Psalms will ask it, even Jesus will cry out in its shadow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their children are established and their offspring are in sight—the wicked inherit continuity, family, future. Job's children are dead. This isn't abstract theology; it's the raw sight of injustice that cuts deepest: they keep what matters most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The rod of God is not upon them." Job sees no divine punishment visiting the wicked. Their houses are safe. This is what troubles him most—the silence of judgment, the apparent absence of the God who should care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even their livestock thrive. Prosperity flows from their herds, no miscarriage, no loss. It's the small, relentless accumulation of blessing on undeserving hands. Job knows this kind of wealth—and now he watches from outside it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their children dance; little ones run in flocks. The wicked know the simple joy of abundance and family laughter. Job hears that laughter and sees its absence in his own tent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They sing to tambourine and harp. The words echo Isaiah and David—joy, music, feasting. These instruments appear in Solomon's court, in celebration before the Lord. Yet here they belong to the wicked. The deepest unfairness is that evil knows pleasure too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They spend their days in prosperity, then suddenly go down to Sheol. Death comes swift for them—no lingering bed of suffering like Job's own drawn agony. Even the mercy of a quick end goes to the wicked.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Depart from us." The wicked actively reject God's company, and God apparently obliges—leaving them to their prosperity uninterrupted. Job's problem is not rebellion; it's that he begs for God's presence and finds Him distant anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They ask, "What profit if we pray?" and get no answer—which itself becomes their answer: none visible, none promised. Their refusal seems rewarded by success. Job, who prays, sees no visible profit either. Where's the difference?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Their prosperity is not in their hand." Job sees the paradox: the wicked didn't earn it themselves, yet they hold it. Meanwhile, he once held prosperity in an open hand, offered it to God—and God took it. The hand that gave is the hand that takes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job poses his question to his friends: "How often is the lamp of the wicked put out?" He wants them to count, to observe with honesty. The answer, he believes, is "not often enough." And the silence that follows is unbearable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Like stubble before wind, like chaff in a storm—Job quotes images of judgment his friends would know, but notes they rarely match what he actually sees. The wicked stand firm. The storm passes over them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job mocks their doctrine: "God lays up sin for the wicked man's children." But he's seen this too—righteous and wicked alike pass suffering to their heirs. This promise of delayed justice hasn't kept him from his own grave-bound state.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let his own eyes see his destruction. Let him drink the wrath of the Almighty." Job frames what should happen—judgment, ruin, divine anger poured out. His words become a prayer. But prayers, he knows, may go unanswered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "What does he care for his house after him?" The wicked man enjoys his day and dies—his months cut off cleanly, his care ended. Job's months stretch before him as a slow continuation of ruin. This, too, is unfair.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Shall any teach God knowledge?" Job turns their logic back on them. They claim to speak for God, to instruct Job in divine ways. But they've never stood where Job stands, seen what he sees, suffered what he bears. Who among them judges the Most High?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One man dies in full strength, at ease and quiet—not diminished as Job has been. The contrast is nakedly unfair: one dies whole, his body still alive with vigor, while another withers and despairs. There is no cosmic balance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "His pails full of milk." Job paints the scene of a man who lived well all his days—nourished, thriving, his very bones soaked through with vigor and vitality. This man feared nothing and lacked nothing. Then death took him anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Another dies in bitterness of soul, never tasting good. Job mirrors one fate against another—both end in death, but one knew only suffering, the other knew joy. What fairness is there in that distance between them?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "They lie down alike in the dust." Death erases the difference. The man of ease and the man of bitterness both feed the worm. In the grave, their fates converge—but by then it matters nothing. The bitterness was lived first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I know your thoughts." Job sees through his friends' comfortable reasoning. They are searching for ways to prove he deserved this, that there is hidden sin, a hidden reason. He rejects both their pity and their judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent of the wicked?" His friends may point and say, "See, they are destroyed," but Job asks: have you actually looked? Can you show me? Or do you only imagine their ruin?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Haven't you asked wayfaring men?" Job challenges them to get evidence, to check with travelers who move between lands and see what actually happens. Talk to those who carry real knowledge, not doctrine.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The evil man is reserved for calamity, led out to wrath—this is what the travelers attest. But when? In this life? The next? Job demands the timing, the visible proof his friends claim.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Who shall declare his way to his face? Who shall repay?" Job poses the unanswered question: in this life, the wicked rarely face judgment for their deeds. How then can his friends speak with such confidence?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He will be borne to the grave. Men shall keep watch over the tomb." Even in death, the wicked receive honor—a procession, a watch kept, a remembered place. The grave itself becomes a kind of throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The clods of the valley shall be sweet to him. All men shall draw after him." Job uses the image of harvest and ripeness—the grave accepts the wicked man as earth accepts seed, returning sweetness. They are mourned and followed. What dignity death grants to the wicked.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo of this when they face a system that rewards the corrupt, or watch the comfortable prosper while the faithful suffer. Job's question remains: where is God's justice? We do not answer it with platitudes either. We sit with him and admit the silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
